name: The Reed household — a documented joiner in a reconstructed household (north division)
head: inf_joiner_north_02

arrival.note: NOT AN ARRIVAL, A BOUND. Nothing dates a hypothesised household, and a year would be a claim nobody made. `not_later_than` the scene date states the only thing the inference carries: the town's need is measured on 1 July 1835, so the household is posited as being here by then and at no stated time before it.

party_size_on_arrival.note: Not claimed. The layer infers households, not families: the person entries here are the ones the trade argument requires and nothing counts wives or children, because counting them would multiply a hypothesis by an invention.

origin.note: Not claimed. Where a hypothesised resident came from is unknowable by construction, and the documented layer's origins (Vermont, Washington, Ann Arbor) are evidence about those men and not a distribution to sample from.

reason_for_coming.note: Not claimed for the person. The reason the HOUSEHOLD is in the dataset is the trade argument in research_note, which is a statement about the town and not about a motive.

lives_at.note: THE HOUSEHOLD IS HOUSED, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE LAYER. recon_1835_north_d4_004 is an anonymous reconstructed roof already standing on the plat, adopted rather than duplicated: its existence, position and footprint stay conjectural and the adoption adds only the occupant argument. Which roof of the right family and district a hypothesised household occupies is not evidence about that roof; the household needed a dwelling and the programme assigned it one.

works_at.note: NO SEPARATE WORKPLACE. A joiner in this town worked in other people's buildings, in the street, or in the dwelling itself, and inventing a shop for the sake of a link would be inventing a building.

present_on_scene_date.note: Presence on the scene date IS the hypothesis: this household exists in the dataset because the town of 1 July 1835 demonstrably needed households of this trade. It is not a finding about anybody's whereabouts.

persons.name: J. W. Reed

occupation.note: THE PAPERS NAME HIM A JOINER. 1833-12-31 c002 (p. 3, col. 3): “WANTED, T[WO] or THREE Journeymen Cabinet M[a]k[ers], to whom good wages will be paid by J. W. REED. Chicago, Dec. 11, 1833.”. The corpus names him 1 time(s), 1833-12-31 to 1833-12-31. THE HOUSEHOLD'S OWN ARGUMENT IS UNCHANGED and is why this roof is in the dataset at all: The finish half of the building trade - doors, sash, stairs, counters and shop fronts - which the reconstruction schedule names in the same family as the carpenter (W2, 'carpenter or joiner shop') and which the documented layer does not hold at all. A town raising two-storey stores with glazed fronts on South Water and Lake employs men who do nothing else.

persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON IN A RECONSTRUCTED HOUSEHOLD, AND THE TWO HALVES OF THAT ARE GRADED SEPARATELY. The person is real and the papers name him: 1833-12-31 c002 (p. 3, col. 3), and 1 mention(s) between 1833-12-31 and 1833-12-31. WHERE HE LIVED AND WORKED IS STILL RECONSTRUCTED — the dwelling, the workplace and the division on this record are the ones the inferred-household programme dealt to the invented resident this replaces, and NOTHING HERE CLAIMS THEY ARE HIS. No source this project holds gives him an address; if one did, the register would have placed him and tools/retire_invented_residents.py would have refused him for that reason (refusal 5). This is what T-0264 retires: the town raised this household because it demonstrably needed the trade and had nobody documented to put in it, and it now has somebody. The invented name and its `name_basis` are gone with the invention. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1); the liberty taken is the housing, not the man.

research_note: RECONSTRUCTED HOUSEHOLD - second of 2 joiner households in this layer, in the north division. The finish half of the building trade - doors, sash, stairs, counters and shop fronts - which the reconstruction schedule names in the same family as the carpenter (W2, 'carpenter or joiner shop') and which the documented layer does not hold at all. A town raising two-storey stores with glazed fronts on South Water and Lake employs men who do nothing else. METHOD: the count comes from the occupation census in data/reconstruction/1835_inferred_household_programme.json, which calibrates every trade against three things this project already holds - the 1835 town census (3,265 people, 398 dwellings), Andreas's roster of the fall of 1833 (about fifty named people, most with a trade, in a settlement of some 350), and the reconstruction specification's roof schedule, whose workshop and store family targets are treated as the ceiling on a trade rather than as its measure. Every count is stated NET of the documented layer: this dataset infers a tradesman only where it cannot name one.
